chunks: And whatever is narrated from Muhammad ibn Al-Husayn ibn Abi Al-Khattab, I have narrated it from my father; and from Muhammad ibn Al-Hasan - may Allah be pleased with them - from Sa'd ibn Abdullah; and Al-Himyari; and Muhammad ibn Yahya, and Ahmad ibn Idris, all together from Muhammad ibn Al-Husayn ibn Abi Al-Khattab Al-Zayyat, and the name of Abi Al-Khattab is Zayd.

key_terms.أَبُو الْخَطَّابِ: Abu Al-Khattab, a kunya (nickname) of the narrator
key_terms.الزَّيَّات: Al-Zayyat, a laqab (title) meaning 'the Olive Oil Seller'
key_terms.رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا: May Allah be pleased with them, a phrase of approval
key_terms.سَعْدُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Sa'd ibn Abdullah, a prominent Shia scholar
key_terms.مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ الْحُسَيْنِ: Muhammad ibn Al-Husayn, a key narrator

ai.seo_question: Who are the narrators in the chain for Muhammad ibn Al-Husayn ibn Abi Al-Khattab?
ai.summary: This passage from *Man La Yahduruhu al-Faqih* provides a critical isnad verification for narrations attributed to Muhammad ibn Al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab al-Zayyat, explicitly linking them to Shaykh al-Saduq’s own teachers, including Abu al-Husayn and his son Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. By citing a diverse group of reliable transmitters such as al-Humayri and Ahmad ibn Idris, al-Saduq reinforces the scholarly consensus and authenticity of these reports within the Ja'fari tradition.
